Paper: Goodfellow et al. (2014), [Generative Adversarial Nets](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.2661).
A GAN learns a generator by training it against a discriminator that distinguishes data examples from generated samples.
The generator defines a distribution through its samples, without requiring an explicitly evaluated data likelihood.

## Problem

Let $z\sim p_z$ be an easy-to-sample random input and let $x=G_\theta(z)$ be a generated example.
These outputs have an induced distribution $p_g$, even when its density is unavailable in closed form.
The task is to make that distribution resemble the data distribution $p_{\mathrm{data}}$ using only samples and differentiable networks. [Paper, §§1–3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1406.2661#page=1).

## Previous attempts

Likelihood-based latent-variable models can require difficult marginalisation or approximate inference.
Some undirected models require sampling procedures during training to handle normalising constants.
The original GAN framework instead obtains its training signal from a learned discriminator and samples through a forward pass of the generator. [Paper, §§1–2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1406.2661#page=1).

## Proposed solution

The discriminator outputs $D_\psi(x)\in[0,1]$, interpreted as the probability that its input came from the data source rather than the generator under the training mixture.
Define the two parts of the value function as

$$
  V_{\mathrm{real}}=\mathbb E_{x\sim p_{\mathrm{data}}}\log D_\psi(x),
$$

$$
  V_{\mathrm{fake}}=\mathbb E_{z\sim p_z}
  \log(1-D_\psi(G_\theta(z))).
$$

The original minimax objective is

$$
  \min_\theta\max_\psi
  \left(V_{\mathrm{real}}+V_{\mathrm{fake}}\right).
$$

The discriminator maximises correct source classification, while the generator minimises the value obtained on its own samples.
Training alternates parameter updates instead of solving an entire inner optimisation to completion at every iteration. [Paper, Eq. (1) and Algorithm 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1406.2661#page=3).

For the discriminator, minimising the negative value function is binary cross-entropy with real labels one and fake labels zero.
For the generator, the original minimax loss can have weak gradients when the discriminator strongly rejects generated examples.
The paper therefore also proposes the non-saturating generator loss

$$
  L_G^{\mathrm{NS}}
  =-\mathbb E_{z\sim p_z}\log D_\psi(G_\theta(z)).
$$

This is a changed generator objective with the same desired equilibrium, not an algebraic rearrangement of the minimax loss. [Paper, §3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1406.2661#page=3).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation: why the alternative gives a stronger early gradient"}

Let $a$ be the discriminator logit for one generated sample and $D=\operatorname{sigmoid}(a)$.
For the minimax generator term,

$$
  \frac{d}{da}\log(1-D)=-D.
$$

For the non-saturating term,

$$
  \frac{d}{da}[-\log D]=D-1.
$$

When $D$ is near zero, the first derivative is near zero but the second is near minus one.
These are derivatives with respect to the discriminator logit; the full generator gradient also contains the derivatives of the discriminator and generator maps.

:::

## Evidence and the ideal optimum

For a fixed generator and an unrestricted discriminator, the optimal discriminator is

$$
  D^*(x)=\frac{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)}
  {p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)+p_g(x)}.
$$

Substituting it into the minimax value gives

$$
  V(D^*,G)=-\log4
  +2D_{\mathrm{JS}}(p_{\mathrm{data}}\Vert p_g).
$$

The global minimum therefore occurs at $p_g=p_{\mathrm{data}}$, where $D^*=1/2$ on their support.
This is an ideal distribution-space result under the paper's assumptions, rather than a guarantee that finite neural networks trained by alternating gradients converge. [Paper, Proposition 1 and Theorem 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1406.2661#page=4).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation: optimal discriminator and Jensen–Shannon divergence"}

At a fixed point, let $a=p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)$ and $b=p_g(x)$.
Maximising the discriminator value reduces to maximising

$$
  h(D)=a\log D+b\log(1-D).
$$

For $a,b>0$, differentiation gives

$$
  h'(D)=\frac aD-\frac b{1-D}=0,
  \qquad D^*=\frac a{a+b}.
$$

The minus sign arises from differentiating $\log(1-D)$, and $h''(D)<0$ confirms a maximum.
Boundary cases with one density zero use the corresponding endpoint value of $D$.
Set $M=(p_{\mathrm{data}}+p_g)/2$ and substitute the optimum:

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  V(D^*,G)={}&-\log4\\
  &+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{\mathrm{data}}\Vert M)\\
  &+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_g\Vert M).
  \end{aligned}
$$

By definition, half the sum of those two KL terms is the Jensen–Shannon divergence.
The resulting divergence identity applies to the original minimax value with an optimal discriminator; it does not make every practical non-saturating update exact Jensen–Shannon descent.

:::

The paper also evaluates generated samples on MNIST, Toronto Face Database, and CIFAR-10.
Its reported likelihood comparisons use Parzen-window estimates, which the authors explicitly identify as having limitations. [Paper, §5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1406.2661#page=6).

## Limitations

The generator and discriminator must remain sufficiently coordinated for their gradient signals to be useful.
A generator can map many inputs to a limited set of outputs, producing poor coverage of the data distribution.
The original framework does not provide a tractable data density or an inference network mapping each observation back to a latent code. [Paper, §6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1406.2661#page=7).
Fast feedforward sampling and difficult training are separate properties; neither establishes a universal ranking against other model families.

## Connections

[VAE](vae.qmd) trains a latent-variable model with a variational likelihood bound, whereas [normalizing flows](normalizing-flows.qmd) track densities through invertible maps.
[DDPM](ddpm.qmd) and [flow matching](flow-matching.qmd) generate through repeated denoising or numerical integration.
These are overlapping choices about model representation, training objective, and sampler, rather than one exhaustive partition by neural architecture.
The [model terminology note](../../study-notes/machine-learning/generative-models.qmd#generative-models) compares these classification axes.
The [cross-entropy study](../../study-notes/mathematics/entropy.qmd#cross-entropy) explains the discriminator's supervised classification loss.
